newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FEATURE-S.Africa seeks to rebuild KwaZulu as peace holds.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-S.Africa seeks to rebuild KwaZulu as peace holds.

text.p: An eight-month-old peace between Nelson Mandela's African National Congress and largely tribal Inkatha Freedom Party is holding, but a massive refugee problem is threatening efforts to rebuild the country's Zulu stronghold.

Half a million internal refugees have fled the fighting between the two factions, which began more than a decade ago, and remain the biggest threat to an enduring stability, independent violence monitors cautioned.

Some 14,000 people were killed in the conflict which at its height forced up to a million people to flee their homes. While many have since returned to home there are still around 500,000 displaced people in the province.

"People who were displaced by political violence and have not been able to go home are most definitely a threat to peace in KwaZulu-Natal. People are still displaced and the situation is critical," peace worker Danny Chetty told Reuters.

"The greatest problem is that abandoned homes now have other people living in them and given that some homes have been occupied for many years, it could generate a lot of tension when the original owners want to move back," he said.
CASH HANDOUT SWEETENS CONCILIATION
Mandela's government has focused on attempts to stabilise the region since his party won power in the 1994 all-race polls ushering in democratic rule.

Seen as a potentially renegade province within an otherwise stable republic, KwaZulu-Natal is run by Inkatha -- South Africa's biggest black opposition party which is campaigning for a federal system and entrenched rights for tribal chiefs.

A conciliatory Mandela has however wooed the Zulu monarch, King Goodwill Zwelithini, into adopting a non-political stance and has successfully brought Inkatha's leader Mangosuthu Buthelezi into government where he is Minister of Home Affairs.
Mandela again moved towards reconciliation when he named Buthelezi, his once bitter rival, as acting president for a day in January when he and his deputy, Thabo Mbeki, were abroad.

In another push towards a lasting peace the South African government has now allocated 100 million rand ($23 million) in its proposed budget for 1997/98 to peace initiatives in KwaZulu-Natal, and specifically to deal with the refugee problem.

The ANC has said the money will also be spent on orphans of political violence and to rebuild houses destroyed in fighting. Many of the political refugees currently live in sprawling shanty towns which have mushroomed on the outskirts of cities.
FUTURE LIES WITH ELECTIONS AS DEATHS TAPER OFF

The low-key civil war, which peaked just before the elections, has tapered off from well over 100 deaths a month to February's recorded death toll of 14, according to the independent Human Rights Committee (HRC).

Researcher Makubetse Sekhonyane said progress was evident with the level of attacks declining, but he warned that "no-go zones" -- party strongholds where rival supporters are not welcome -- are still cause for concern.
"The number of people being displaced has gone down considerably since the decline in the number of attacks on homesteads which caused many people to flee from those areas," he told Reuters.
"There is still some displacement happening but not on the same large scale as a few years ago. It is still a problem, however," Sekhonyane said.
Buthelezi has already begun to ready his party for a tough fight in the next general election, scheduled for 1999.

But political analysts are sceptical that he will turn around his party's fortunes, saying it has little support outside KwaZulu-Natal, home to nine million Zulus. The party won only 10 percent of the national vote in the last election.
Alexander Johnston of the University of Natal's politics department told Reuters the party would have to shed Buthelezi as its leader if it wanted to spread its powerbase.
"The quite uncompromising hostility felt by many African people towards Buthelezi means that as long as he is leader it will be quite impossible," he said.
